cards.explanation: The answer is Jerusalem. The Spirit lifts Ezekiel, a priest among the exiles (Ezekiel 1:1, 3), up between earth and heaven and carries him there in visions of God (Ezekiel 8:3). No walking, no packing, no asking if we're there yet. I got carried once myself, from a kitchen counter to the back of a junk drawer, and that trip took a hand and a slammed drawer.

The answer is the idol that provokes jealousy. The text says it was seated at the entrance of the north gate of the inner court (Ezekiel 8:3). God then tells Ezekiel to lift his eyes to the north, and he sees this idol of jealousy in the entrance north of the Altar Gate (Ezekiel 8:5). So Ezekiel sees it twice.

The answer is the glory of the God of Israel. Ezekiel says it was like the vision he had seen in the plain (Ezekiel 8:4). So even here, at a gate with an idol at it, he sees that glory. I think that's a big moment for Ezekiel, and it's worth slowing down for, friends.

The answer is True. God asks Ezekiel if he sees what they are doing, the great abominations the house of Israel is committing, and He says they do it “…to drive Me far from My sanctuary?” (Ezekiel 8:6). This is a heavy part, friends, and I won't make light of it. God is showing Ezekiel something painful, and He says there's more to see.

The answer is even greater abominations. God says, “Yet you will see even greater abominations.” (Ezekiel 8:6). The idol at the gate isn't the end of the tour, friends. Ezekiel has only just started walking.

The answer is False. God tells Ezekiel, “dig through the wall.” and no peeking is involved (Ezekiel 8:8). Ezekiel digs, and on the other side he discovers a doorway. That's a lot more work than a quick look, friends.

The answer is seventy elders of Israel. Ezekiel sees them standing before the engravings, and Jaazaniah son of Shaphan is named among them (Ezekiel 8:11). Each one has a censer in his hand. Seventy is a lot of people to find in one hidden room, friends.

The answer is False. The elders are saying, “The LORD does not see us; the LORD has forsaken the land.” (Ezekiel 8:12). They say it while they're in the darkness, each at the shrine of his own idol. I think the darkness is part of the picture, friends.
The answer is forsaken. The elders say, “the LORD has forsaken the land.” (Ezekiel 8:12). That's what they say, in the darkness, each at his own idol's shrine. Those are their words, friends.

The answer is women. At the entrance of the north gate of the house of the LORD, Ezekiel sees women sitting there, weeping for Tammuz (Ezekiel 8:14). Tammuz is a false god. It's a quiet scene after the crowded room, friends.

The answer is False. About twenty-five men stand between the portico and the altar, but they have their backs to the temple of the LORD and their faces toward the east (Ezekiel 8:16). So they're turned away from it. I think that's the detail to notice, friends.

The answer is the sun. About twenty-five men have their backs to the temple of the LORD and their faces toward the east, and they're bowing in worship of the sun (Ezekiel 8:16). It's a sad sight, friends. I'll just say it plainly.

The answer is throughout the whole land. God asks if the abominations they practice there aren't enough, “…that they must also fill the land with violence and continually provoke Me to anger?” (Ezekiel 8:17). So it's the whole land, not just the temple. Violence in the land is what God names, friends.

The answer is with wrath and no pity. God says, “Therefore I will respond with wrath. I will not look on them with pity, nor will I spare them.” (Ezekiel 8:18). I won't joke about this one, friends. Take a quiet breath before the next one.
The answer is True. God says, “Although they shout loudly in My ears, I will not listen to them.” (Ezekiel 8:18). That's the last line of the passage. Let it sit a moment, friends.
